Content:
I mean, you can all shit on the 8gb GPUs, but as long as they continue to be priced reasonably below their other models (i mean ffs, the 5060 is $180+ cheaper than the 5060 TI 16gb version as of writing this), i will continue to buy those shitty models. It's a little frustrating seeing videos like these because i feel like you guys miss the core reason as to why "budget" gamers are getting absolutely fucking shafted in the modern PC market: The fact that you guys continued to buy GPUs from 2018 onward that were ridiculously over priced for what they were. You guys all implicitly told Nvidia and AMD that it was OK to jack up their prices and not aim for large performance upgrades because you, frankly assholes, couldn't stop yourselves from upgrading every year to the next big thing. 

You guys want to keep attacking the companies going "hurr durr company bad company raise prices" while completely ignoring the personal responsibility that comes with "hurr durr monkey see big price monkey still buy!". 

This isn't to excuse the companies. Nvidia and AMD are scum companies cheating their consumers out of reasonably priced tech. But NONE of that will be fixed if the consumer doesn't wake the fuck up and stop buying the 70, 80, 90 classes of Nvidia GPUs and the higher end AMD shit. Frankly Transient spikes should have been the fucking death knell for modern tech and the fact that you all bought enough to collectively say "nah we like this" is fucking embarrassing.

I'm not in the extreme enthusiast end of the market in PCs (any more), however I think the "culture" of MSRP may work differently in the US and in the UK and perhaps elsewhere.

I think the overt dishonesty that's sunk into this part of the market has got to a stage now where the GPU makers might actually mislead some people, but to many people who see this, they're now nothing more than a parody. A meme of themselves.

Author: @BoltHardcheese
Content:
Honestly, at this point MSRP is strictly to entice people to go to the store (retail or online). Once there, most people are unable to buy at MSRP, as manufacturers never really wanted to sell many at that price point. They purposely only make a few at that desired price point, similar to a retail store advertising a black Friday deal for a 4k TV but only having 10 in stock at that price. The point is not to offer people a good deal, it's to get them in the door.

They are counting on the human tendency to not want to leave empty handed, so purchasing the next closest thing. You go to the store or online, all the $600 cards are sold out, so you then panic and think these are really selling out fast, I need to buy something before they are all gone. You then go past your normal comfort level and overspend. Some of us are immune to this; I for one saw there were no $600 cards and promptly gave up and closed my browser, resigning myself to try again at the next GPU launch. However, this method clearly works for the majority, as stores have been doing this for years for a reason. Capitalism will always try to upsell you.

Author: @nocturnal101ravenous6
Content:
So here is my take - Please articulate any comments as to why I am wrong.
Ai/enterprise is ruining both the CPU and GPU markets as well as the non-volatile Flash market, Fab lines are so congested creating enterprise level products that making consumer level products has become unprofitable and its the main reason for mass stagnation across multiple segments.
1- GPUs - Don't know what to do with themselves, 1080 high refresh is obviously the most used resolution with probably the Prosumers using Ultrawide 3440x1440p OLED panels standards like HDMI2.1 and DP 2.1 are past the bandwidth capability of the GPUs abilities same goes for PCIe standards for a while now, Multi-GPU configs are a danger to the overall Product Market tier stacking which we won't see SLI/Crossfire make a comeback is because it would destroy their product stacks now that CXL PCIE5 basically fixed the issues of old MultiGPU configs. AMD/NVidia/Intel are so consumed with fake frames created by AI that they have no actual; incentive to produce actually decent Graphics cards or to change the formula as we know it, we do not have enough graphical power for full Ray Traced rendering moving from Rasterization, so we are left with this bastardized current iteration. Once you get to 8k at 240htz with a 99.5% color accurate OLED, the market is done, you have reached the capabilities end of what the medium can do unless something radical comes along to change things, I would say at this pooint VR will eventually become the standard.
2- CPUs - They topped out, the industry knows once you reach a certain level, at the current OS kernel designs you are never going to see real progress that matters until Silicon is transitioned to something like Photonics and that change means you can have a complete overhaul of the standards that are now bogging down the industry as a whole. There is only so far you can go and CPUs are basically now just Frankensteins between gate layers nm, I/O nm, and the actual transistors nm.
3- Volatile Ram - in the next 5 years Camm2 will overtake the market its going to be the new transition. It will be the new hotness.
4- Motherboards - Have become a waste of space market with things we all pay for and never use, Why does my x670e ProArt have onboard audio that is substandard? I don't know considering any creative Professional will be using a Focusright scarlet or competing product at minimum so why does my Mobo not have something like a native Thunderbolt chip on the board instead? Something I can actually use, maybe to justify a $500 price tag? Its literally the least effort BS products on the market and the sad fact is you have to choose 1, I don't want dongle life for the motherboard using PCIe riser cards people don't have room in the cases for configurations.
5- Non-Volatile Ram - We are currently stagnated on consumer levels its really really bad, M.2 has basically topped out PCIe5 at 4TB TLC, Manufacturers have stopped trying, 2.5 the last decent drive was the Crucial MX500 4TB TLC drive and they stopped making them by this point we seriously should have 10-15TB consumer drives, we are still paying the same price for the same silicon just with increased speeds with Flash increasing capacity at the cost of endurance levels by increasing bits per cell, its still an SLC drive at 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 the capacity on higher bits per cell storage and they have stagnated into the current capacities with no actual increases that have led to price fixing with 8TB being $600-1000 for 5+ years.
6- HDD market - A price fixed garbage market of charging $500 for 24TB despite speed being subpar, reliability being subpar, and the industry doing everything it can to cut corners with clear deceptions and garbage practices, begging to be over regulated into oblivion by governments and trade markets.
7- LCD - another constantly price fixed market despite ho-hum actual progress. 4k OLED ultrawide HDR with 1200+nits and perfect black? Where is it? Its been a F&*king Decade of Ultrawides - closest is the new LG panel coming around but they skimped on resolution, they have sandbagged the market so badly GPU manufacturers have literally no incentives to even bother trying to keep up, Why am I paying $1k for an Premium ultrawide that is subpar compared to HDTVs atm when literally you are getting 4 panels for the same level of manufacturing of a TV, and the only reason HDTVs suck is the lack of real HDMI2.1 and DP2.1 as inputs.

Author: @carlr2837
Content:
People all forget that the value of the dollar has fallen 13% this year. If you adjust for a constant dollar, most models of GPU are actually selling at or below the adjusted MSRP, and this is in addition to any effect of tariffs. Manufacturers should make an official adjustment to MSRP to reflect this, but since MSRP is only a one-time guess as to where the selling price will end up, and completely irrelevant after launch day, they don't bother. The falling dollar is, however, reflected in the price they charge the AIB makers for the chips, and the prices that the AIB makers pay for other components, such as memory, fans, etc. and the labor to assemble the boards, since none of that is in the US. No doubt it also affects the prices the store have to pay for the boards as well, and thus, ends up in the final price consumers pay, like it or not.
5060 Ti-16 Original MSRP $429, MSRP in constant dollars $489, current best price $429 ($60 under)
5070 Original MSRP $549, MSRP in constant dollars $625, current best price $599 ($26 under)
9070 Original MSRP $549, MSRP in constant dollars $625, current best price $599 ($26 under)
9070XT Original MSRP $599, MSRP in constant dollars $683, current best price $699 ($16 over)
5070 Ti Original MSRP $749, MSRP in constant dollars $853, current best price $824 ($29 under)
5080 Original MSRP $999, MSRP in constant dollars $1138, current best price $1299 ($161 over)
5090 Original MSRP $1999, MSRP in constant dollars $2278, current best price $2499 ($221 over)
One this is for sure - you can see that it matters when AMD has no competition (i.e. 5080 and 5090).

Author: @BassDXX
Content:
I really enjoyed this video, but to be honest as someone with a science background, it's really important to point out that you can't make as many useful conclusions from all this data because you are only looking at one snapshot in time. This analysis would be far more useful if it also showed data from multiple points in time, such as moving averages and trends. What interests me most is seeing how prices have changed from launch and are continuing to change, and I can tell you that looking at the used market and also on PC Partpicker, it seems like AMD cards (particularly the 9070 XT) are slowly trending downward in price, while Nvidia pricing remains pretty sticky. I have observed that several people who bought a 9070 XT this generation only did so because they couldn't get a 5080 at launch, only to later sell it once they were able to get one.

Frankly, I don't really understand why any rational human being would do this. The 5080 has to hands down be one of the worst value GPUs of all time, even more so than all the 8 GB 60 class cards that you all seem to love dunking on. 5090 prices are more ludicrous, but at least that card has its place as the undisputed best. On the other hand, the 5080 isn't that much faster than the 5070 Ti/4080S/9070 XT while costing waaaay more. Meanwhile for all of the flack they have gotten from reviewers, the 5070 and 9070 (non-XT) have consistently given the best performance per dollar among all mid to high end cards, yet people continue to overlook them.

Author: @Kraaketaer
Content:
Thanks for the super interesting coverage, even if it's just yet more depressing confirmation of things we already knew.

For anyone interested in a perspective from a small non-US market, here's how things stand currently in Norway:
- When most of the recent GPUs launched, the USD-to-NOK conversion rate was ~1:11.3. From that, the 9070 XT has seemingly been consistently availble around MSRP (when also accounting for our 25% VAT) - there are models in stock at ~9000NOK as we speak (compared to the currency converted+VAT "MSRP" of ~8500), and these have been available regularly. The problem is that the currency conversion has changed dramatically since then (currently around 1:10), while GPU prices have not really followed, even if overall pricing has dropped slightly, and today the "MSRP" would be ~7500NOK. So, 9070 XTs are up 20% minimum, and many models are much, much higher than that.
- For 5070 Tis the situation is essentially identical, just shifted up by ~2000NOK - there is a single model available at ~10 000NOK, but most are well above that - the "premium" models here are especially egregious.
- I also spotted several models of the 9060 XT 16GB being sold for a price essentially exactly matching US MSRP*conversion rate+25% - but only for the first three days, before they jumped up by ~500NOK and stayed there. Whether this was an error on the side of the stores, an adjustment in an official guidance, or something else, I have no idea - I just hope a bunch of people jumped on that "deal" while it was available. Since they launched later the conversion rate changes aren't affecting the relative pricing as much there, but there's still a ~12% upcharge over MSRP minimum.

From what I've seen, this is pretty representative overall. Now, some lag between currency fluctuations and price changes is understandable, but still ... I'm so, so happy I'm not in the market for a GPU right now.

Author: @ShayLC
Content:
There's lots of different ways to do averages, and I don't think that giving equal weight per model is an accurate representation of what consumers are paying. I was watching the stock numbers at microcenter and noticed that one particular model (the steel legend 9070 xt, at $700) seemed to be restocked more often and to significantly higher stock quantities than more expensive models of the same card. Usually the very expensive ones had only 1-3 cards, while the cheaper ones stocked 20-30 at a time when shipments arrived. The more expensive ones also rarely seemed to restock the same model frequently, where in the lower end price range I'd see the same models restocked. In my trip to microcenter, I also saw 4 people buying 9070XTs, all of whom chose the $700 card over the various other models which were available at higher prices and had only one of each model on the shelf. This makes sense both because a lower volume model will cost more per unit than a high-volume model, and because basic economics says consumers will buy higher quantities at lower prices. 

I won't claim to know what the best approach is to calculating the data, but I will claim to know that weighting the different model numbers equally in your calculations without factoring in what volume they're sold at is going to skew the price estimations towards higher prices than what consumers are actually paying on average per card sold.

Content:

Content:
The difference between MSRPs and the various other prices that manufacturers are suggesting for their GPUs interests me. 

Not the difference in prices, mind you. What interests me here are the semantics—which the manufacturers clearly don't understand. They are aware of what the "M" and the "S" in MSRP stands for, right? Me? I'm just not sure they do. 

For anyone that doesn't know—and also isn't bothered to look it up—MSRP stands for "Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price", hence my interest in the matter, as well as my confusion and consternation. How can a manufacturer set an MSRP for a product, and then suggest a price for the product to their vendors that is _not_ the MSRP? Doesn't this defeat the purpose of MSRP?

Content:
I payed 590€ for an MSI RTX 3070 Gaming X Trio back at the end of 2020. 8GB VRAM GPU. Good price. good card (I was amazed at the performance coming from a GTX 860M, 4 GB VRAM laptop GPU). Sadly it died due to humidity a little before warranty was over (lucky me).

With the generational leap it should have been cheaper and Steve said something among the lines "performance good, product bad cause price bad". Also, remember, the 4070 Ti is the "unlaunched 4080 12 GB", said 4080 12 GB was supposed to be for 100 USD MSRP higher, what a scam Nvidia was gonna pull there. And even with that reduction in MSRP it still had a bad price.

I made the math, checked the performance charts... The 4070 Ti I ended up buying had around 150% performance (average FPS in various games) for 150% price (590€ vs 930€, redoing the math just now, it's 157%). I even tried a 6800 XT for less than 2 weeks and didn't like it (AMD drivers, multi monitor, coil whine). I bit the bullet and bought it and justified to myself it being a RTX 3170... 

Lo and behold, one year later (2023) Nvidia launched the 4070 Ti Super. Same MSRP price, 16 GB of VRAM instead of 12 GB of VRAM. I was so mad. AMD is also launching budget and mid tier 16 GB VRAM products (and have good drivers now, FIX YOUR SH*T NVIDIA).

In conclusion, 8 GB VRAM is basically a scam. There was good products with 8 GB VRAM 5 years ago. Not now.

You are forgetting a use case where peoples actually buy 8GB GPU because they are the cheaper available while still being performant enough for their usage : dedicated GPU for framegen or upscaling with lossless scaling in a dual gpu configurations.
